This is an AI benchmark review, not an assessment of human participants. Only the supplied extraction and benchmark passage were used; the authoritative PDF was not independently inspected. Ratings retain EFPA meanings: n/a = inapplicable; 0 = insufficient information to rate; 1 = inadequate; 2 = adequate; 3 = good; 4 = excellent. A 0 does not establish poor instrument quality. Section judgments use reasoning, not averages. No aggregate benchmark-quality score is calculated.

Part A, section 1 — Factual description. Reviewer: AI adopting the assigned benchmark-reviewer perspective; no human credentials claimed. Current review date: not supplied. Previous review date: not supplied; sources were inspected on 7 October 2026, which is not necessarily a review date. Instrument name: ARC-AGI-2 public test problems, official scoring software and ARC Prize verified-testing rules. Short name: ARC-AGI-2. Original test name for a local adaptation: n/a; no local adaptation identified. Original authors: ARC Prize Foundation staff and partners; François Chollet and colleagues are credited for the illustrated technical report, but a complete authorship list is absent. Local adaptation authors: n/a. Local distributor/publisher: ARC Prize is the identified evaluation organization; formal distributor details are absent. Original publisher if different: unspecified. Current edition publication date: unspecified. Local adaptation publication date: n/a. Original publication date: unspecified.

Section 2 — Classification. 2.1: Other: novel-rule inference, grid problem solving, abstract reasoning. These are intended constructs, not established comprehensive intelligence measures. 2.2: Other: AI evaluation and research. 2.3: AI systems; eligible architectures and population boundaries are unspecified. 2.4: Intended users are not explicitly classified; researchers can inspect public materials. 2.5: One reported problem-averaged score; no established distinct-skill subscales. 2.6: Other: machine-produced output grids; precise interface requirements are absent. 2.7: Human attention, language fluency, digital experience, handedness, hearing, motor capabilities, reading, vision and writing are not literal prerequisites for an AI. Handedness, hearing and physical motor requirements are n/a. Attention as a psychological prerequisite is n/a. Command of test language, language fluency, digital skills, reading, vision and writing require reinterpretation as instruction processing, interface compatibility, grid perception and structured output; relevant limitations are information missing. Other: representing grid dimensions and colours is necessary, but supported encodings are unspecified. 2.8: Verified tests specify settings and spending limits, record conditions and use one run; exact settings and limits are absent. Development training is allowed, evaluation-specific tuning discouraged, and repeated feedback optimization is restricted. 2.9: Production-based grid output and task success in a computer-generated environment; no evidence that latency is itself a scored response type. 2.10: Coloured two-dimensional grids; exact digital stimulus encodings are unspecified. 2.11: 1,000 development problems and three evaluation sets of 120 each; new inputs per problem vary, with no minimum, maximum or typical count supplied. 2.12.1: Individual AI-system evaluation is the functional interpretation; batch/group administration is unspecified. 2.12.2: Automated, controlled evaluation is described for verified tests; human proctor and identity categories lack literal counterparts. Public testing conditions can differ. 2.13: Software is available; precise hardware, connectivity and proprietary apparatus requirements are unspecified. 2.14: Preparation time unknown; human administration time unknown, although the test is automated; scoring is automated, implying 0 manual scoring time under EFPA guidance, not zero computation time; analysis and stakeholder feedback times unknown; debriefing an AI has no established counterpart. 2.15: Development, public, semi-private and private sets; ARC-AGI-1 is a separate version. Human difficulty matching does not establish parallel AI forms. Validity of using subsets independently is unspecified. 2.16: Published fixed problem sets; no adaptive generation described. 2.17: Other: the evaluated AI produces task responses, rather than human self-report; human solvers informed development.

Section 3 — Measurement and scoring. 3.1: Digital scoring of AI outputs. 3.2: Two attempts per new input; exact dimensions and every colour must match for credit. Input credits are averaged within problems, then problem scores are averaged. This differs from the documentation's whole-problem 'fully solved' designation. No guessing correction is described. 3.3: Other: mean task-credit proportion; no established standard scores or decision thresholds. 3.4: n/a; no standard-score transformation identified. 3.5: No differentiated norms documented; this is not proof that no reference information exists elsewhere.

Section 4 — Digitally generated reports. 4.1: Digital scores and claimed publication of outputs, costs, times and problem scores are documented; availability and number of EFPA-style interpretative reports are unknown. 4.2: Evaluation score/output records; formal report names absent. 4.3: Presentation format unknown. 4.4: Problem-level and overall numerical structure; construct-based narrative structure unestablished. 4.5, 4.6, 4.7, 4.8, 4.9, 4.10: Context sensitivity, report-development process, modifiability, score-to-text transparency, interpretative content and intended recipient classifications unknown. Applying these questions to numerical evaluation records is an explicit reinterpretation, not evidence that interpretative reports exist.

Section 5 — Supply arrangements. 5.1: Technical report, task instructions, public problems, software, scoring tests and dated change record are described; formal user manuals and support groups unspecified. 5.2: Public digital releases and documentation; exact distribution formats unspecified. 5.3: Supplier qualification requirements unspecified, not explicitly 'none'. General description: ARC-AGI-2 asks AI systems to infer transformations from example grid pairs and produce new output grids. Public development problems support practice; three evaluation sets have different access restrictions. Exact-match input credits contribute to a problem-averaged score. Verified evaluations specify settings and spending constraints. Human puzzle-solving data informed selection and difficulty matching. The stated purpose includes comparing unfamiliar-grid problem solving and investigating broader reasoning claims; no AI norm tables, competence thresholds or established distinct-skill subscales are supplied.

Part B — Sources: the supplied passage only, summarizing inspected materials; no confidential publisher information was reviewed. Ratings refer to this packet, not an independent audit.

Section 6 — Rationale and documentation. 6.1.1=2: Rule inference from examples has an intelligible operational rationale; its connection to general intelligence is not established. 6.1.2=2: Human piloting and AI results are summarized, but detailed construct research is absent. 6.1.3.1=2: Examples, exact outputs and controlled evaluation fit grid-solving comparisons; justification of all design choices is incomplete. 6.1.3.2=2: Newly written and unused puzzles, developer review and duplicate-rule removal provide content-development evidence. 6.1.3.3=2: Selection and human difficulty matching are described, but final-pool item analyses and detailed decision criteria are absent. 6.1.4=n/a: No translated/local adaptation identified. 6.1.5: Framework not specified; human difficulty information described; no numerical item difficulty, discrimination, DIF or other psychometric indices supplied. 6.1.6=2: Human piloting and rule review constitute basic item evaluation, but AI-focused analysis depth is unestablished. 6.1.7=0: Final-set item statistics insufficient to evaluate difficulty spread, discrimination or floor/ceiling effects. 6.1.8=2: Basic rationale and development procedures are supported; this does not establish AI item psychometrics.
6.2.1=2: Intended grid-solving construct and design rationale are understandable. 6.2.2=2: Sources, piloting and corrections are outlined without complete development records. 6.2.3=n/a: No local adaptation. 6.2.4=2: Verified conditions are outlined, but exact standardization protocol is absent. 6.2.5=0: No interpretable norms or explicit sole-ranking exemption documented. 6.2.6=0: No repeated-test precision estimates. 6.2.7=2: Content-selection rationale is described; expert numbers, qualifications and quantitative agreement are incomplete. 6.2.8=0, 6.2.9=0, 6.2.10=0: Internal-structure, external-variable and additional validity studies are insufficiently documented. 6.2.11=0: AI group-comparability guidance absent. 6.2.12=0: Report reliability and validity documentation absent. 6.2.13=0: The summarized passage does not permit assessment of language throughout user documentation. 6.2.14=2: Basic task, scoring and development information is usable, with substantial technical omissions.
6.3.1=2: Attempts and verified-testing controls are outlined, without complete procedural troubleshooting. 6.3.2=2: Formula, exact matching and selected marking tests are described; complete marking verification is absent. 6.3.3=0: Norming instructions absent and applicability unresolved. 6.3.4=2: Narrow score meaning and whole-problem terminology distinction are available; uncertainty-based interpretation is absent. 6.3.5=0: Stakeholder feedback guidance absent; human-style AI debriefing is n/a. 6.3.6=0: AI fairness/bias-use guidance absent. 6.3.7=2: Development versus evaluation use and feedback restrictions are specified, but eligible-system restrictions are incomplete. 6.3.8=0: Hardware, error handling and technical support details insufficient. 6.3.9=0: Complete supporting references and cross-references unavailable. 6.3.10=2: Basic procedures are interpretable despite missing operational detail. 6.4=2: Adequate basic rationale and documentation, without demonstrated technical adequacy for broad claims.

Section 7 — Materials. 7.1.1=0: End-to-end robustness and failure recovery untested in this packet. 7.1.2=2: Demonstrations and output goal make the task specification understandable; model comprehension is not established. 7.1.3=2: Examples and practice tasks exist, but complete interface instructions are absent. 7.1.4=0, 7.1.5=0: Ease of machine response and interface quality cannot be established. 7.1.6=n/a for human disability accessibility; AI interface/representation accessibility would be a different question, with insufficient evidence. 7.1.7=2: Structured grid content and ongoing corrections support basic material quality; known unclear examples preclude stronger judgment. 7.1.8=2: Adequate basic digital task materials, with software operation insufficiently assessed. 7.2.1=n/a, 7.2.2=n/a, 7.2.3=n/a, 7.2.4=n/a, 7.2.5=n/a, 7.2.6=n/a, 7.2.7=n/a: No paper or physical administration identified. Comments: corrected squares and unclear examples are documented; completeness and score impact of corrections are unresolved.

Section 8 — Norms. 8.1.1=n/a, 8.1.2=n/a, 8.1.3.1=n/a, 8.1.3.2=n/a, 8.1.3.3=n/a, 8.1.4=n/a: No norm-referenced score interpretation is identified; AI or human sample counts cannot be treated as norm samples. 8.2.1.1=n/a, 8.2.1.2=n/a, 8.2.1.3=n/a, 8.2.1.4=n/a, 8.2.1.5=n/a, 8.2.2=n/a: No competence cut score or standard-setting exercise identified; exact answer keys are not competence thresholds. 8.3.1=n/a, 8.3.2.1=n/a, 8.3.2.3=n/a: No identified norms whose age, distortions or fair-use properties can be assessed. 8.3.2: Acceptable norms are not demonstrated. 8.3.2.2: EFPA permits a no-norm exception for an explicitly sole raw-score-ranking purpose; this packet also discusses broader interpretation and does not establish that restriction. 8.3.3=0: Overall norm adequacy is unresolved under that guidance, not demonstrated inadequate. A documented sole-ranking use could justify n/a instead. Human difficulty matching is not AI norming.

Section 9 — Reliability/precision. 9.1: No coefficients or measurement-error estimates supplied. 9.2.1=0, 9.2.2=not specified, 9.2.3=0, 9.2.4=no information: Internal-consistency evidence absent; whether a coherent item scale supports this method is unestablished. 9.3.1=0, 9.3.2=0, 9.3.3=no information, 9.3.4=no information: No identical-condition AI retest sample, coefficient, interval or population match supplied. Section 10 — Validity. 10.1: Content evidence is evaluated under 6.1 and 6.2.7, as EFPA directs. It supports grid-domain relevance, not comprehensive intelligence coverage. 10.2.1=no information, 10.2.2=0, 10.2.3=0: No factor structure, justified alternative dimensional analysis, invariance or DIF evidence supplied; a psychological factor interpretation is not assumed. 10.3.1.1: Human background-group analysis is described; equivalent AI validation designs are absent. 10.3.1.2=0: No justified AI-group hypotheses and effects supplied; absence of a clear human background association is not AI validity evidence. 10.3.1.3=0, 10.3.1.4=0: No convergent/discriminant correlations, marker reliabilities or justified hypotheses supplied; no correlation anchors can be applied. 10.3.1.5=n/a: No MTMM design identified. 10.3.1.6=0: No systematic AI manipulation study of instructions, presentation or software. 10.3.1.7=n/a: No additional external-variable design identified. 10.3.1.8=0, 10.3.1.9=0, 10.3.1.10=unknown, 10.3.1.11=0: AI validation sample sizes, marker quality, study ages and overall external-variable evidence unresolved. 10.3.2.1=not established, 10.3.2.2=0, 10.3.2.3=0, 10.3.2.4=0, 10.3.2.5=n/a, 10.3.2.6=unknown, 10.3.2.7=0: No predictive, concurrent or postdictive external criterion study supplied; no diagnostic application identified. Section 11 — Supporting fair use. Here AI groups mean relevant system classes and evaluation conditions, not human protected identities; this adaptation does not assess downstream fairness to people. 11.1.1=0, 11.1.2=0: Cross-system construct relevance and inclusion guidance insufficient. 11.2=2: Public practice and controlled verified conditions provide basic comparison provisions; inclusive AI interface design is unestablished. 11.3=0: Human piloting does not supply AI subgroup item analyses. 11.4=0, 11.5=0: Comparable subgroup precision and validity unestablished. 11.6.1=n/a, 11.6.2=n/a: No norm-reference or competence-threshold interpretation identified. 11.7=0: Report bias guidance absent. 11.8=0: Overall fair-use support across AI system groups cannot be established. Human background findings do not establish AI fairness or accessibility.

Section 12 — Digitally generated reports. 12.1=0, 12.2=0, 12.3=0, 12.4=0, 12.5=0, 12.6=0, 12.7=0: No three score-profile reports with actual scores supplied, so coverage, interpretative consistency, validity, bias, acceptability, detail and overall quality cannot be evaluated. These are provisional insufficient-information ratings for potential interpretative reporting; if only numerical records exist, narrative-specific questions become n/a. The illustrative 0.5 calculation is not an observed report profile. Complete archives were not checked.

Final evaluation: The task and scoring procedure support a bounded description of exact grid-solving performance under recorded conditions. Public inspection, practice separation, human-informed selection and revision tracking are strengths. Corrected examples, exposure uncertainty, unquantified repeatability and unvalidated broader interpretations limit conclusions. Score precision and validity of intended interpretations are critical; their 0 ratings trigger EFPA's restriction to research or exceptional expert use for those unsupported purposes, without asserting demonstrated poor performance. Conclusions: Use for research comparisons tied to the specific set, version, scoring formula and evaluation conditions; broader intelligence conclusions and precise ranking differences remain unsupported by this packet. Users need technical evaluation and measurement expertise; agreement with supplier qualification requirements is unknown.

Final evaluation: Authentic engineering materials and explicit task families make DesignQA useful for exploratory analysis of these tasks. Its documented marking errors, uniformly compliant subset, unequal information supply and incomplete replication links restrict interpretation of the overall number and fine ranking differences. Broad engineering competence or transfer to other documents is not established. Reliability and validity are critical; their 0 and 1 ratings trigger EFPA's restriction to research or exceptional expert use for unsupported interpretations. Conclusions: Use for research reporting task-specific results with exact input supply, version and scoring conditions disclosed; interpret the composite cautiously and avoid unsupported general engineering-competence conclusions. Users need engineering-domain, scoring-software and measurement expertise; correspondence with supplier qualification requirements is unknown.
